title: Emergencies at the chair
placement: Module 9, section `bedside` (First actions while help is coming); disequilibrium content from `predialysis`
job: A. The learner recognizes five time-critical dialysis emergencies and knows the first actions for each, especially the ones where blood must not be returned.
alt: Reference card of five dialysis emergencies (air entry, hemolysis, needle dislodgement, dialyzer reaction, disequilibrium), each with signs and first actions.
caption: In every emergency, call for help early, stay with the patient, and record the onset time. In hemolysis and severe dialyzer reactions the blood in the circuit is not returned, and blood is never returned through a line that contains air. Oxygen, positioning, and further steps follow the unit’s emergency protocol.
reviewer_flags: Left-lateral head-down positioning is "traditional consensus practice; confirm against unit protocol" (m09 FLAGS).

title: The peritoneal membrane and transport type
placement: Module 10, section `membrane` (The membrane in depth: why the same bag behaves differently in different people)
job: U. The learner sees that the capillary wall is the real filter, why the glucose pull fades during a dwell, and why fast and slow transporters need different prescriptions.
skill: williamriveromd-biomedical-mechanism-figure (+ Constitution v1.0 Layer A, Tenckhoff rules)
alt: Diagram of the peritoneal capillary wall with two kinds of opening, the fading glucose pull, and the shapes of fast and slow transporter curves.
caption: Water and small solutes cross the peritoneal capillary wall through gaps between cells, and water alone crosses through tiny water-only channels. Glucose leaks back into the blood, so the pull on water fades. This happens sooner in fast transporters, which is why they do better with short dwells.
reviewer_flags: The plan's layers "interstitium" and "mesothelium" do not appear in the module text, so they are left out. The module uses the capillary wall model only. Curves are drawn as shapes only, with no numbers on the axes.

title: The exchange: the reason behind each step
placement: Module 10, section `exchange` (The exchange: the reason behind each step)
job: A. The learner can teach and audit a twin-bag exchange in the right order and say why each step exists, especially the flush before the fill.
skill: williamriveromd-simple-figure (Scaffold C) + Constitution v1.0 Tenckhoff rules
alt: Five-step twin-bag peritoneal dialysis exchange shown as labeled flow paths (connect, drain, flush, fill, disconnect), with the reason for each step and how to record net removal.
caption: The flush comes before the fill because it carries any organisms picked up at the connection away to the drain bag before fluid flows toward the abdomen. Net fluid removal equals the volume drained minus the volume filled.
reviewer_flags: The module puts the deep cuff "in the abdominal wall muscle", while the Constitution says "preperitoneal". The label follows the module, and the drawing places the cuff deep in the wall just outside the peritoneum. The module gives no distance in centimeters for the superficial cuff, so none is labeled. Fill volume (about 2 L) is left out because it is not needed.

title: Cloudy fluid or abdominal pain: the peritonitis pathway
placement: Module 10, section `infection` (Infection in depth: exit site, tunnel, and peritonitis)
job: A. The learner knows what to do, in order, from the phone call about cloudy fluid through specimen collection, treatment and follow-up, and when catheter removal comes up.
alt: Five-step card for suspected PD peritonitis: contact the team now, assess and collect specimens, the three diagnostic criteria, prompt treatment, and reassessment.
caption: Cloudy fluid or abdominal pain means contacting the PD team now. Peritonitis is diagnosed when at least two of three criteria are met; specimens are collected before antibiotics when feasible, and prescribed treatment starts without waiting for culture results.
reviewer_flags: FOR CLINICIAN REVIEW. The ">100/µL", ">50% neutrophils", "≥2 hours", "5 days" (refractory), "4 weeks" (relapsing) and "2–3 days" values were written from recall and are flagged in the module (FLAGS line 1); confirm them against the ISPD 2022 text. The ISPD unit rate targets (≤0.40 episodes per patient-year; culture-negative <15%) are in the module but are left off the image because they are a program standard, not a bedside step. Treatment is shown only as "per program protocol", with no drug names.

title: Where the new kidney sits, and what can go wrong there
placement: Module 11, section `physiology` (From referral to the first week)
job: U. The learner pictures the graft joined to the pelvic vessels and bladder, and links each join to the complication and bedside sign it can produce.
skill: williamriveromd-biomedical-mechanism-figure (+ Constitution v1.0 Layer A vessel and ureter rules)
alt: Lower-abdomen diagram of a transplanted kidney joined to a pelvic artery, pelvic vein and bladder with a stent, labeled with each site's warning sign.
caption: The new kidney is placed in the lower abdomen and joined to the pelvic vessels and the bladder. Each join has its own complication. Because the graft has no nerve supply, a blocked ureter is often painless, and a clot in the artery can stop urine abruptly.
reviewer_flags: The module does not name the iliac fossa, the right side, the external iliac artery or vein, or whether the native kidneys stay in place. The labels therefore say "pelvic artery", "pelvic vein" and "lower abdomen", and the view is cropped below the native kidneys so the image makes no claim about them. The drawing shows standard anatomy (right iliac fossa, external iliac vessels). If Dr. Rivero wants those terms on the image, add a sentence to `physiology` first.

title: Infection after transplant: a timeline
placement: Module 11, section `complications` (Complications: surgical, immune, and infectious)
job: A. The learner matches the months since transplant to the infections to expect and the nursing focus for that window, and remembers that fever is always reported.
alt: Three-window timeline of infections after kidney transplant (first month, months 1 to 6, after 6 months) with the nursing focus for each window.
caption: Infection risk follows the level of immunosuppression. Opportunistic infections peak in months 1 to 6 and come back whenever immunosuppression is increased to treat rejection. Fever in a recipient is always reported the same day.
reviewer_flags: The module notes that this is the conventional teaching framework and that programs differ in prophylaxis and screening schedules. No prophylaxis agents or durations are shown.

title: Immunosuppressants: what to ask, what to guard against
placement: Module 11, section `drugs` (The immunosuppressants: what to ask about and what to guard against)
job: A/P. The learner can ask about the right side effects for each agent and catch the dangerous interactions, especially azathioprine with allopurinol or febuxostat, and grapefruit or pomelo with tacrolimus-class drugs.
alt: Reference card of six transplant immunosuppressants showing what each does, side effects to ask about, and interactions to guard against. Shows no doses or levels.
caption: A vigilance card, not a prescribing guide. Doses and blood levels are set by the transplant team, and no new medicine, supplement or herbal product is started until the team has checked it.
reviewer_flags: FOR PHARMACIST AND TRANSPLANT PHYSICIAN REVIEW (whole card), per module FLAGS 3 and 4. The cited KDIGO guideline may not be the primary source for the azathioprine and allopurinol/febuxostat interaction. Side-effect lists are shortened selections from the module table, with nothing added. No doses or target levels appear.

title: A worked Plan–Do–Study–Act cycle
placement: Module 12, section `dashboard` (Infection surveillance, the unit dashboard, and improvement methods)
job: A. The learner sees a whole PDSA cycle, from aim and measure through the decision to adopt, on a problem every unit knows: sessions that end early.
alt: Four-part Plan–Do–Study–Act cycle on early-ending afternoon sessions, with aim, measure and decision. All figures are labeled illustrative.
caption: A worked example with invented figures. One small change was tested on one shift for two weeks, measured weekly, and then kept and extended, and a second cycle began on cramps.
reviewer_flags: The "Illustrative figures" label must appear on the image (module FLAGS: invented figures).

title: The unit quality dashboard
placement: Module 12, section `dashboard` (Infection surveillance, the unit dashboard, and improvement methods)
job: P. The learner sees that bedside records feed ten quality domains the unit reviews monthly, and that targets come from the medical director, not from this course.
alt: Grid of ten dialysis-unit quality domains, each with example measures and no targets, plus the infection rate formula per 100 patient-months.
caption: A unit dashboard tracks a small set of measures every month. Each target comes from the guideline the unit has adopted and is set by the medical director. Accurate nursing records are where these reports begin.
reviewer_flags: None. No targets appear, by design (module FLAGS).

title: Typhoon readiness: before, during, after
placement: Module 12, section `readiness` (Disaster and disruption readiness in depth)
job: A/P. The learner knows the nurse's part in each phase of a disaster, and that the first task afterward is accounting for every patient.
alt: Three-phase typhoon readiness sequence for a dialysis unit (before, during, after) with the nurse's tasks and patient teaching for missed dialysis.
caption: Survival after a disaster is mostly arranged before it. Patients are dialyzed early when the nephrologist orders it, every patient is accounted for by name afterward with clinical urgency guiding who is dialyzed first, and treatment restarts only after the water system has been recommissioned and tested.
reviewer_flags: The module gives no quantities for fluid, potassium or reserve supply, and none are shown. Back-up unit arrangements follow each unit's plan.

title: Delegation: tasks you may hand over, judgments you keep
placement: Module 12, section `teamwork` (The dialysis team, delegation, and accountability)
job: A. The learner can tell a delegable task from a nursing judgment and knows the four conditions for safe delegation.
alt: Comparison of tasks a nurse may delegate in a dialysis unit, subject to authorization, training, policy, and supervision, and the judgments that stay with the registered nurse.
caption: A nurse may hand a task, not a judgment, to a trained and authorized technician or assistant under unit policy and supervision. Assessment, the decision to start, and evaluation of the response stay with the nurse, and so does the signature.
reviewer_flags: Which tasks may be delegated, including priming, is set by facility policy and PRC Board of Nursing issuances (module FLAGS 2). The figure says "per unit policy".
